newsitem.title: THAILAND: Ailing Thai bank hopes to recall most bad loans.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Thai bank hopes to recall most bad loans.

text.p: Thailand's troubled Bangkok Bank of Commerce Ltd Plc said on Tuesday it hopes to recall about 60 percent of non-performing loans totalling 56.75 billion baht granted to borrowers for takeover of listed firms in the past.
"We are optimistic we can collect about 60 percent of the bank's bad loans," Thavisak Na Takuathung, BBC's senior executive vice president, told a news conference.

Thavisak was asked by the bank's government-appointed controlling committee to chase the non-performing debt, which form the major portion of a grand total of 77 billion baht ($2.96 billion) in bad and doubtful loans incurred by the BBC.
The government took over BBC in May 1996 to save it from a massive run on its deposits after the bank was found to be saddled with the massive debts.
Thavisak said the major borrowers who failed to repay interest and pricipal included Saudi tycoon Adnan Khashoggi who used the loans to take over listed companies.
Khashoggi had borrowed about five billion baht from the bank, Thavisak said.

Thai police last month issued arrest warrants for Khashoggi on charges of conspiring to defraud the BBC. They also issued warrants for the bank's former president Krirkkiat Jalichandra and its former adviser Rakesh Saxena.
BBC this month plans to auction 4.9 million shares, or the 49 percent stake it has in a cooking oil producer Morakot Industries Plc, as part of its move to recall bad loans, Thavisak said.
Shares of Morakot Industries had been put up as collateral by some borrowers to seek loans for a buyout of Morakot, he said.
BBC previously sold 5.06 million share or 50.6 stake in Morakot to Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby Bhd at 150 baht per share for a total of 759.59 million baht, he said.
The central bank has appointed the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand to manage the bank and take an 18 percent stake in it.
The IFCT is 45 percent owned by the finance ministry and other government agencies. The remainder is in private sector hands.
